reasoning_traces.think:
The causal framework centers on estimating the effect of strategic interventions—specifically, the infield shift—in Major League Baseball. The core estimand is ETT (effect on the treated), defined as the expected difference in run expectancy between plate appearances where the shift was applied versus those where it wasn’t. Three methods are employed: k:1 nearest neighbor matching on propensity scores, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and instrumental variables (IV) with a preference-based instrument. Matching balances covariates to approximate randomization, while IPTW adjusts for selection bias. The IV approach leverages team-level shift propensity as an instrument to isolate exogenous variation in treatment assignment. These methods are triangulated to strengthen inference against unmeasured confounding. The dual nature of the estimand—both observational and counterfactual—requires careful handling of SUTVA violations due to multiple possible shift configurations. Each method operates under distinct assumptions: matching assumes conditional exchangeability, IPTW requires positivity and correct model specification, and IV demands valid instruments and exclusion restrictions. The triangulation logic ensures robustness by requiring agreement in directionality and statistical significance across methods. Failure modes include weak instruments, model misspecification, or violation of exclusion restrictions in IV, and unmeasured confounding in matching or IPTW. The framework thus embodies a dualism between empirical balance and causal identification, with each method serving as a check on the others.
